newsitem.title: TANZANIA: UN suspends night operations for Rwanda refugees.
newsitem.headline: UN suspends night operations for Rwanda refugees.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency said on Wednesday it was suspending indefinitely its night operations helping refugees return to Rwanda after a soldier fired on a U.N. convoy.
U.N. officials said no one was hurt in the incident, which occurred on Tuesday night at a Rwandan checkpoint 19 km (11 miles) inside Rwanda from Tanzania.
The exodus of Rwandan Hutu refugees, ordered out of the country by the Tanzanian government, continued on Wednesday.
"As of midday 17,487 crossed today so we have now reached 225,000 since it began on Saturday," said Paul Stromberg, a spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).
"It is quite clear that the majority of the 540,000 Rwandan refugees in Tanzania before this operation began have already returned to Rwanda or are on their way back," added Stromberg.
UNHCR suspended its night operations after a Rwandan soldier fired on a pickup in a U.N. convoy returning to the Tanzanian border after dropping refugees.
Officials said a truck stopped at a Rwandan checkpoint but its driver did not set the hand-brake so it rolled into the pickup, prompting a soldier to fire.
The pickup driver said three bullets hit his vehicle. One went through the right hand side of the windscreen but the driver was not hit because the pickup had its steering wheel on the left.
"It was an unfortunate incident," said Stromberg, adding UNHCR officials were raising it with the Rwandan authorities.
Aid officials said a large group of refugees was emerging from the bush about 90 km (55 miles) southeast of Ngara and starting the march north towards the Rusumo crossing point into Rwanda.
"These people are ill, cold and hungry -- that's why they are coming out," said UNHCR spokeswoman Judith Melby, adding refugees in the Karagwe region to the north were also heading for the border.
Most of the 125,000 refugees in the Karagwe region will have to walk about 250 km (150 miles) to the Rusumo border crossing.
UNHCR sent field officers on Wednesday to camps for 112,000 Burundian refugees to reassure them that they were not covered by a Tanzanian deadline of December 31 for all Rwandan refugees to go home.
To ensure the mass exodus maintained its momentum, Tanzanian authorities are rounding up suspected Hutu hardliners accused of trying to stop innocent refugees from going back to their homes.
More than 50 babies have been born on the road since Monday and mothers have tied their children to them with pieces of yellow string to avoid losing them in the crush of refugees.
Former Rwandan Hutu Interahamwe militiamen and troops refuse to go back to Rwanda, saying they will be attacked or jailed for their part in the genocide of minority Tutsis in 1994.
The exodus from Tanzania follows the return of an estimated 600,000 Hutu refugees from eastern Zaire, where a Tutsi-led rebellion forced them all to abandon their camps last month.

The refugees left Rwanda in 1994 when troops, militiamen and mobs slaughtered some 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus. Rwandan Tutsi rebels then drove them out of the country and formed the present government.

The bulk of Rwandan Hutu refugees in Tanzania fled away from the border last week after the Tanzanian government set the December 31 deadline for them to go home. But many were turned around by Tanzanian troops and police at times wielding sticks.
